Airline booking

You run the booking system for an airline. Fare searches are heavy, seats are limited, and every flight needs the right number of tickets, no more and no fewer. You depend on a partner system for fares from other airlines, and it has strict limits. A fare sale and a slow partner will both happen on the same day. Practise this hard system design problem for free, with no sign-up.

Play this problem

The brief

You run the booking system for an airline. Fare searches are heavy, seats are limited, and every flight needs the right number of tickets, no more and no fewer. You depend on a partner system for fares from other airlines, and it has strict limits. A fare sale and a slow partner will both happen on the same day.

Think of an airline's booking and seat system.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
20 million visitors a month (approx.)
Audience in plain numbers
20,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 6,000 requests per second
Request mix
Search: 58%; Read: 25%; Write: 6%; Payment: 2%; Sign-in: 6%; Notification: 3%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Search: ≈ 1,500 ms; Read: ≈ 750 ms; Write: ≈ 1,800 ms; Payment: ≈ 4,000 ms; Sign-in: ≈ 1,500 ms
Successful requests
99.95%
Data safety
No acknowledged write may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $53,000
Data at rest
≈ 4 TB
Where users are
North America: 60%; Europe: 40%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Search: 900 seconds; Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Payment: 3,600 seconds; Sign-in: 900 seconds; Notification: 900 seconds
Fresh reads
People must see their own changes. At most 0.1% of reads may be stale in the model.
Personal reads
40% of reads are private; a shared public copy cannot answer them.
Required proofs
Managed encryption keys; Audit trail; Personal data isolated; Tested backups

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • About 3,500 fare searches a second at peak. Seat holds and changes are about 360 writes a second (approx.).
  • A partner (global distribution) system provides some fares; limit about 200 requests a second.
  • All numbers are rough approximations.
  • Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

Questions that shape the design

Can two people hold the same seat?

Never. A seat is held by exactly one person, and holds expire after 15 minutes.

How heavy is a fare search?

Heavy. Most results can be reused for a few minutes, since fares move slowly, except during a sale.

What is the partner system limit?

About 200 requests a second, and during busy hours it can cut that in half without warning.

What records must we keep?

Passenger and payment records are sensitive. Every action must be audited, data encrypted, and backups proven to restore.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 09:30 · Slow dependency

    An outside service slows down. Your servers fill with requests waiting on it.

    Added response time: ≈ 3,000 ms. Duration: ≈ 1,800 seconds.

  2. 12:00 · Flash crowd

    A scheduled launch brings a sudden rush of requests.

    Traffic for Search, Read, Sign-in reaches 6 times the scheduled load; rises over 120 seconds, holds for 1,200 seconds and eases over 1,800 seconds. Other request types keep their scheduled load.

  3. 19:00 · Provider rate limit

    An outside service lowers its configured request quota and answers 'too many requests' above the reduced limit.

    Provider capacity falls to 50% of its configured quota. Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Searching can use old answers. Holding a seat cannot. Where must the seat count live so two people cannot take the same one?
  • Fence seat holds and resolve payments without exceeding partner fare quotas.
  • Sync replication adds a few ms to every seat hold. It is the reason a failover cannot lose a booking.
  • Caching fares for five minutes cuts partner calls by about 90 percent, and shows a price that may be a few minutes old. Re-check the price at checkout.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Which copy is the truth
  • Timeouts and failing fast
  • Proof built in
